tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Accounting – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: Accounting is best defined as the process of:
options: Identifying, recording, classifying, summarising and interpreting financial transactions
questions.explanation: It covers recording through to interpretation of financial information.

questions.question_text: The AICPA (1941) defined accounting as the art of:
options: Recording, classifying and summarising in a significant manner and in terms of money transactions of a financial character, and interpreting the results
questions.explanation: It includes interpretation of the results.

questions.question_text: The American Accounting Association defines accounting as the process of:
options: Identifying, measuring and communicating economic information to permit informed judgements and decisions
questions.explanation: The emphasis is on communicating information to users.

questions.question_text: Book-keeping differs from accounting in that book-keeping is:
options: Only recording of transactions, while accounting also analyses and interprets
questions.explanation: Book-keeping is the clerical base of accounting.

questions.question_text: Which is a feature of accounting?
options: Records only financial transactions measured in money
Is always done by the owner
questions.explanation: Accounting records events that can be measured in monetary terms.

questions.question_text: Accounting is needed because it:
options: Provides information about profit, financial position and helps decision making
questions.explanation: Memory cannot record all transactions reliably.

questions.question_text: Which is an objective of accounting?
options: Ascertaining profit or loss and the financial position
questions.explanation: Others: systematic records, providing information to users.

questions.question_text: The main branches of accounting are:
questions.explanation: Each serves different needs.

questions.question_text: Cost accounting differs from financial accounting in that cost accounting:
options: Ascertains and controls the cost of products and services
Prepares statutory final accounts for outsiders
questions.explanation: Management accounting helps managers in planning and control.

questions.question_text: Which is an internal user of accounting information?
questions.explanation: Owners and employees are also internal users.

questions.question_text: Which is an external user of accounting information?
questions.explanation: Government, investors and tax authorities are also external users.

questions.question_text: A creditor mainly needs information about the firm's:
options: Ability to pay dues (liquidity and solvency)
questions.explanation: They want to know whether the business can repay.

questions.question_text: Investors mainly need information about:
options: Profitability and the prospects of returns on investment
questions.explanation: They decide to invest, hold or sell.

questions.question_text: A function of accounting is:
questions.explanation: Others: determining results, communicating information.

questions.question_text: An advantage of accounting is that it:
options: Helps in ascertaining profit and provides evidence in legal matters
questions.explanation: Records are accepted as evidence.

questions.question_text: A limitation of accounting is that it:
options: Records only monetary transactions and may be affected by personal judgement
questions.explanation: Some figures rest on estimates.

questions.question_text: Accounting cannot record employee skill because it:
options: Cannot be measured objectively in money
questions.explanation: The money measurement concept restricts what can be recorded.

questions.question_text: Accounting concepts are:
options: Basic assumptions on which accounting is based
questions.explanation: They form the foundation of accounting practice.

questions.question_text: Accounting conventions are:
options: Customs or traditions followed to ensure uniformity and comparability
questions.explanation: E.g., consistency, conservatism, materiality.

questions.question_text: Concepts differ from conventions in that concepts are:
options: Fundamental assumptions, while conventions are practices that arise from usage
questions.explanation: Concepts are more basic.

questions.question_text: The fundamental accounting assumptions are:
questions.explanation: As per AS 1.

questions.question_text: Under the business entity concept, the business and its owner are:
questions.explanation: E.g., the owner's personal expenses are not business expenses.

questions.question_text: Drawings reduce capital because:
options: The owner withdraws from the business, a separate entity, which owes capital to him
questions.explanation: They are treated as a reduction in the owner's claim.

questions.question_text: The money measurement concept records only transactions that can be:
options: Expressed in money, which is its limitation as it ignores non-monetary facts
questions.explanation: E.g., morale or skill is ignored.

questions.question_text: The going concern concept assumes the business will:
questions.explanation: Assets are valued on that basis.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Accounting – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: Because of the going concern concept, fixed assets are shown at:
options: Cost less depreciation rather than at forced-sale value
questions.explanation: The business is not expected to sell them soon.

questions.question_text: The accounting period concept divides the life of a business into:
options: Periods (usually a year) to measure profit and financial position
questions.explanation: It enables periodic reporting.

questions.question_text: The cost concept states that assets are recorded at:
questions.explanation: It supports objectivity.

questions.question_text: The dual aspect concept states that every transaction has:
options: Two equal aspects: debit and credit
questions.explanation: The basis of the accounting equation.

questions.question_text: The revenue recognition concept says revenue is recognised when:
options: It is earned, regardless of when cash is received
questions.explanation: AS 9 deals with it.

questions.question_text: For credit sales, revenue is recognised when:
options: Goods are sold and delivered (risk and ownership pass)
questions.explanation: Not when cash is collected.

questions.question_text: The matching concept requires that:
options: Expenses of a period are matched with the revenues of the same period
questions.explanation: It gives a true profit figure.

questions.question_text: The accrual concept means:
options: Revenue and costs are recognised when they occur, not when cash is paid or received
questions.explanation: It is the basis of mercantile accounting.

questions.question_text: Under the cash basis, transactions are recorded when:
questions.explanation: Accrual records when earned or incurred.

questions.question_text: The objectivity concept means that accounts should be based on:
questions.explanation: Bills and vouchers support entries.

questions.question_text: The consistency convention requires:
options: The same accounting methods to be used from period to period
questions.explanation: It allows comparison across periods.

questions.question_text: The conservatism convention means:
options: Anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses
questions.explanation: Example: provision for doubtful debts.

questions.question_text: Stock is valued at cost or market price, whichever is lower, because of:
questions.explanation: Anticipated losses are recognised but not anticipated gains.

questions.question_text: The materiality convention says that:
options: Only significant items need separate disclosure; trivial items can be ignored
questions.explanation: E.g., small stationery may be expensed.

questions.question_text: Full disclosure means:
options: All material information should be disclosed in financial statements
questions.explanation: Users should not be misled.

questions.question_text: The accounting equation is:
questions.explanation: Capital = Assets − Liabilities.

questions.question_text: Assets are:
options: Resources owned by the business with future economic benefit
questions.explanation: E.g., cash, building, stock.

questions.question_text: Fixed assets differ from current assets in that fixed assets are:
options: Held for long-term use, while current assets are converted into cash within a year
questions.explanation: E.g., land versus debtors.

questions.question_text: Goodwill and patents are examples of:
questions.explanation: They have no physical existence.

questions.question_text: Fictitious assets are:
options: Expenses not yet written off, shown as assets (e.g., preliminary expenses)
questions.explanation: They have no real value.

questions.question_text: Liabilities are classified into:
questions.explanation: E.g., creditors versus debentures.

questions.question_text: Capital is the amount:
options: Invested by the owner in the business
questions.explanation: Drawings are amounts withdrawn by the owner.

questions.question_text: Purchase of machinery is:
questions.explanation: It gives benefit over several years.

questions.question_text: Deferred revenue expenditure is:
options: Revenue expenditure whose benefit extends over several years, e.g., heavy advertising
questions.explanation: It is written off over more than one period.

questions.question_text: The sale of old machinery is a:
questions.explanation: Sale of goods is a revenue receipt.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Accounting – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: Debtors are persons who:
questions.explanation: Creditors are those to whom the business owes.

questions.question_text: Trade discount differs from cash discount in that trade discount is:
options: Allowed on the list price and not recorded in books; cash discount is for prompt payment and recorded
questions.explanation: Cash discount is shown in the books.

questions.question_text: A bad debt is:
options: An amount due from a debtor that cannot be recovered
questions.explanation: It is a loss to the business.

questions.question_text: Started business with cash Rs 1,00,000. Effect:
questions.explanation: Cash and capital both increase.

questions.question_text: Purchased furniture for cash Rs 20,000. Effect:
options: One asset +20,000 and another asset −20,000, so total assets unchanged
questions.explanation: Furniture increases and cash decreases.

questions.question_text: Purchased goods on credit Rs 30,000. Effect:
questions.explanation: Both sides rise by 30,000.

questions.question_text: Paid creditors Rs 10,000. Effect:
questions.explanation: Both fall by 10,000.

questions.question_text: Paid rent Rs 2,000. Effect:
questions.explanation: Rent is an expense that reduces capital.

questions.question_text: The owner withdrew Rs 5,000. Effect:
questions.explanation: Drawings reduce capital.

questions.question_text: Took a bank loan Rs 50,000. Effect:
questions.explanation: Cash and loan both rise.

questions.question_text: Sold goods costing Rs 8,000 for Rs 10,000 on credit. Effect:
questions.explanation: Debtors +10,000, stock −8,000, profit Rs 2,000 adds to capital.

questions.question_text: Assets Rs 5,00,000 and outside liabilities Rs 1,50,000. Capital is:
questions.explanation: Capital = Assets − Liabilities.

questions.question_text: Capital Rs 3,00,000 and liabilities Rs 80,000. Total assets are:
questions.explanation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

questions.question_text: Assets Rs 2,40,000 and capital Rs 1,60,000. Liabilities are:
questions.explanation: Liabilities = Assets − Capital.

questions.question_text: Opening capital Rs 1,00,000; profit Rs 40,000; drawings Rs 10,000. Closing capital is:
The extended accounting equation is:
options: Assets = Liabilities + Capital + Revenue − Expenses − Drawings
questions.explanation: It includes profit and drawings.

questions.question_text: The single entry system is:
options: An incomplete system that does not record the dual aspect of every transaction
questions.explanation: Mainly personal accounts and cash book are kept.

questions.question_text: The double entry system records:
options: Both the debit and credit aspects of every transaction
questions.explanation: Every debit has an equal credit.

questions.question_text: The father of double entry (1494) is:
questions.explanation: He is an Italian mathematician.

questions.question_text: A feature of double entry is that:
options: Every transaction has two aspects, debit and credit
questions.explanation: It ensures a complete record.

questions.question_text: An advantage of double entry is that it:
options: Allows preparation of a trial balance and checks arithmetical accuracy
questions.explanation: It gives a complete record.

questions.question_text: A limitation of double entry is that it:
options: Cannot detect errors of principle or compensating errors
questions.explanation: The trial balance may still agree.

questions.question_text: The difference between single and double entry is that double entry:
options: Is a complete system with two aspects, single entry is incomplete
questions.explanation: Double entry is scientific.

questions.question_text: A trial balance is not possible in single entry because:
options: Only one aspect is recorded, so debits and credits cannot be compared
questions.explanation: There are no equal totals to compare.

questions.question_text: Profit under single entry is ascertained by:
options: Statement of affairs method (comparing capital at two dates)
questions.explanation: Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Accounting – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: Accounts are classified into:
questions.explanation: The basis of the golden rules.

questions.question_text: Of Cash A/c, Rent A/c, Ram's A/c, Capital A/c, Furniture A/c, Commission Received A/c, the nominal accounts are:
questions.explanation: Cash and Furniture are real; Ram's and Capital are personal.

questions.question_text: The accounting process starts with:
options: Identifying and recording transactions in the journal
questions.explanation: Then ledger, trial balance and final accounts.

questions.question_text: The correct order of the accounting cycle is:
options: Journal → Ledger → Trial balance → Final accounts
questions.explanation: Recording, classifying, summarising.

questions.question_text: A voucher is:
options: A document that is evidence of a transaction
questions.explanation: Examples: receipt, invoice.

questions.question_text: Source documents include:
options: Invoices, cash memos and bank statements
questions.explanation: They support entries.

questions.question_text: GAAP stands for:
questions.explanation: The rules followed in preparing accounts.

questions.question_text: The main source of GAAP in India is:
options: Accounting standards issued by ICAI, the Companies Act and other laws
questions.explanation: Also guidance notes.

questions.question_text: The role of ICAI is to:
options: Issue accounting standards and regulate the profession
questions.explanation: The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India.

questions.question_text: Ind AS differs from AS in that Ind AS are:
options: Converged with IFRS and apply to specified companies
questions.explanation: AS are the earlier Indian standards.

questions.question_text: IFRS stands for:
questions.explanation: Issued by the IASB.

questions.question_text: The Companies Act, 2013 requires companies to:
options: Maintain books of account and prepare financial statements in prescribed form
questions.explanation: Section 128 deals with books of account.

questions.question_text: NFRA is:
questions.explanation: It oversees auditing and accounting standards.

questions.question_text: AS 2 deals with:
questions.explanation: Inventories are valued at lower of cost and net realisable value.

questions.question_text: AS 6 deals with:
questions.explanation: It covers allocation of depreciable amount over useful life.

questions.question_text: AS 9 deals with:
questions.explanation: It prescribes when revenue is recognised.

questions.question_text: Financial statements include:
questions.explanation: They show results and position.

questions.question_text: ICDS stands for:
questions.explanation: They are used for computing taxable income.

questions.question_text: "Substance over form" means:
options: Transactions are accounted for by their economic reality, not legal form
questions.explanation: E.g., a finance lease treated as purchase.

questions.question_text: The financial year in India runs from:
questions.explanation: It is the accounting year for most businesses.

questions.question_text: Window dressing is:
options: Manipulating accounts to show a better financial position than the true one
questions.explanation: It is unethical.

questions.question_text: Accounting policies are disclosed so that:
options: Users can understand how figures were prepared and compare them
questions.explanation: AS 1 requires disclosure.

questions.question_text: Profit differs from cash in that profit is:
options: Revenue less expenses on accrual basis, while cash is actual money available
questions.explanation: A business can be profitable but short of cash.

questions.question_text: Cash basis for companies is:
options: Not permitted; companies must follow the accrual basis
questions.explanation: The Companies Act requires accrual accounting.

questions.question_text: Which is an example of capital expenditure?
questions.explanation: Revenue expenditure: wages, rent, salaries.
